facts.statement: Aiolornis lived from the Early Pliocene to the Late Pleistocene.
The species was first described in 1952 by Howard based on a cuneiform bone.
facts.quote: First described as Teratornis incredibilis by Howard in 1952 based on a cuneiform bone

facts.statement: Campbell, Scott, and Springer moved the species to the new genus Aiolornis in 1999.
facts.quote: the species has been moved to the new genus Aiolornis by Campbell, Scott and Springer in 1999

facts.statement: The genus name Aiolornis comes from the Greek words aiolus (god of the wind) and ornis (bird).
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from the ancient Greek words aiolus and ornis

facts.statement: The first material was a cuneiform bone found in Smith Creek Cave, 34 miles north of Baker, Nevada.
facts.quote: The first Aiolornis material, described in 1952, was a cuneiform bone found in Smith Creek Cave, White Pine County, which is located 34 miles north of Baker, Nevada

facts.statement: The holotype specimen is around 40% larger than the corresponding bone in Teratornis merriami.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen (on which the species is based) is around 40% larger than the same bone in T. merriami

facts.statement: A partial humerus collected at Quintin Lake in April 1993, about 1 km northeast of Murrieta, California, was referred to the species.
facts.quote: The 1999 paper also refers a new bone to the species, a partial humerus (upper arm bone). The specimen was collected at Quintin Lake in April 1993, which is located approximately 1 km northeast of Murrieta, Riverside County, California

facts.statement: Scientists are uncertain if all the material belongs to Aiolornis because the fossils are fragmentary and span a large timespan.
facts.quote: There is also a lack of certainty on whether all of this material actually belongs to Aiolornis, due to the fragmentary nature of the fossils and the large timespan they represent

facts.statement: Only fragmentary remains of Aiolornis have been found.
facts.quote: Only fragmentary remains have been found

facts.statement: Aiolornis had an estimated wingspan of 5 to 5.5 meters and a weight of around 23 kg.
facts.quote: Its wingspan is estimated to have been between 5 and 5.5 meters, and its weight at around 23 kg

facts.statement: Aiolornis differs from Teratornis most obviously in its size.
facts.quote: Aiolornis differs from Teratornis in a number of places, most obvious of which is size

facts.statement: The facies articularis ulnaris in Aiolornis is slightly more concave than in Teratornis, with a lower dorsal rim than ventral rim.
facts.quote: The facies articularis ulnaris is also slightly more concave than that of Teratornis, with the dorsal rim lower than the ventral rim

facts.statement: In Aiolornis, the facies dorsalis is fairly flat along the M. latissimus dorsi attachment and becomes slightly convex near the distal end.
facts.quote: the facies dorsalis is fairly flat for the length of the attachment of the M. latissimus dorsi, becoming slightly convex near its distal end

facts.statement: Aiolornis is classified in the family Teratornithidae within the order Cathartiformes.
facts.quote: Aiolornis is classified within Teratornithidae, which is a family in the order Cathartiformes

facts.statement: The order Cathartiformes includes both extinct and extant New World vultures.
facts.quote: The order also includes the extinct and extant New World vultures

facts.statement: The time range for Aiolornis is from the Zanclean to the Calabrian, approximately 4.7 to 1.4 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Zanclean to Calabrian (4.7 to 1.4 million years ago)
